re-pogona-vitticeps.title: Bearded Dragon
re-pogona-vitticeps.summary: A calm, curious desert lizard from central and eastern Australia and one of the most popular first reptiles. It needs a big, hot, brightly lit enclosure with strong UVB and a diet that shifts from mostly insects as a baby to mostly vegetables as an adult.
rows: 18–24 in (45–61 cm) snout to tail tip; males are usually larger. Full grown at 1–2 years
One adult: 6 × 2 × 2 ft (L × W × H) minimum, or at least 24 cubic ft, with about 3 ft of climbing height if possible
Basking surface 108–113°F (42–45°C), cool side 77–85°F (25–29°C). Nights 55–75°F; a drop at night is fine
Strong UVB is required: UVI about 4.0–4.5 at the basking spot, from a T5 HO UVB tube on the warm side

Omnivore. Babies: insects daily plus a daily salad. Juveniles (under 12 in): 5–6 head-sized insects a day plus vegetables. Adults: 3–4 insects twice a week and vegetables 3× a week. Dust with calcium; add a multivitamin 1–2× a week
Usually tolerates handling well once settled. Give it about 2 weeks to adjust before handling, then build trust with short daily sessions
Active by day; basks, climbs and digs
Central and eastern Australia (semi-arid desert, scrub and dry forest)
notes: Keep one per enclosure. Two males will fight, a male and female will breed, and adults may injure or eat smaller dragons.
Overfeeding insects as an adult can lead to obesity and gout; the share of insects should drop as the dragon grows.
Color and scale morphs (red, leatherback, pastel and others) are all this species and share the same care.

re-iguana-iguana.title: Green Iguana
re-iguana-iguana.summary: A giant, tree-climbing, plant-eating lizard from Mexico to southern Brazil. Babies are small and bright green, but adults reach 5–7 ft and live 15–20+ years, so a full-grown iguana needs a room-sized enclosure. Plan for that before buying.
rows: Males can reach 6–7 ft (1.8–2.1 m) including the tail; females rarely pass 5 ft (1.5 m)
One adult: 10 × 5 × 6 ft (L × W × H) minimum. A 4 × 2 × 4 ft enclosure only works briefly for a juvenile; they grow fast
Basking surface about 120°F (50°C), general air 75–88°F, night 73–84°F
60–80% by day, rising toward 100% at night; mist morning and evening
UVB required (UVI 3.0–4.0 at the basking spot) plus very bright grow-style lighting, 12–13 hours a day
Herbivore: about 60% dark leafy greens, 30% other vegetables and 10% fruit. Juveniles and adults can be offered as much as they will eat daily
Active by day; spends most of its time high in the enclosure
Mexico south to southern Brazil and Paraguay; invasive in many warm regions
notes: Males should never be housed together; groups need a much larger enclosure and can still fight.
Albino, red and other color forms are the same species with the same care.
warn: Grows to 5–7 ft and needs a 10 × 5 × 6 ft enclosure as an adult.

re-uromastyx-geyri.title: Saharan (Red) Uromastyx
re-uromastyx-geyri.summary: A small, brightly colored spiny-tailed lizard from the rocky Sahara (Algeria, Mali and Niger) that comes in red and yellow phases. Like all uromastyx it is a true heat-lover and a plant-eater that needs very hot basking, strong UVB and low humidity.
rows: About 11–14 in (28–36 cm) total; around 250 g as an adult. One of the smaller uromastyx
Uromastyx can live over 25 years with good care
4 × 2 × 2 ft (L × W × H) minimum for one; front-opening with good ventilation
Very low: about 20–30%. Offer a slightly moist burrow area in the deeper substrate, with the top inch kept dry
Strong UVB required: UVI 4.5–6.0 at the basking spot, plus bright white light
Herbivore: about 90% greens and flowers (e.g. collard, mustard, dandelion, turnip greens), ~5% hard vegetables/treats, ~5% dry foods. Juveniles daily, adults 4–5× a week
Active by day; basks even in the hottest part of the day, climbs rock stacks and digs burrows
Rocky desert in Algeria, Mali and Niger (central Sahara)
notes: Best kept one per enclosure; pairs or one male with females need at least double the space and may still not get along.
Red and yellow phases differ only in color.

re-anolis-barbatus.title: Cuban False Chameleon
re-anolis-barbatus.summary: A large, slow-moving, chameleon-like anole from western Cuba, prized for its calm nature. In the wild it eats mostly snails, so captive-bred snails should be part of its diet along with insects.
rows: About 7 in (18 cm) snout to vent, plus a thin tail slightly shorter than the body
Tall, front-opening, well-ventilated terrarium: 18 × 18 × 36 in (L × W × H) minimum for one
Basking area about 90°F, cool side 72–82°F, night 65–72°F
High: averages around 80%, from about 40% by day up to 100% at night
UVB recommended at UVI around 2.0–3.0 in the basking area, plus a bright ~6500K LED; 13 h light in summer, 11 h in winter
Mostly snails in the wild. Offer captive-bred snails plus a variety of insects (crickets, roach nymphs, black soldier fly larvae, hornworms, silkworms)
Active by day but sedentary; spends most of its time sitting still on branches
notes: House one per enclosure to avoid fights.
Unlike most anoles, it cannot drop its tail.

sources.name: ReptiFiles – Cuban False Chameleon Care Sheet

re-anolis-equestris.title: Cuban Knight Anole
re-anolis-equestris.summary: The largest anole: a big, bright green, tree-dwelling lizard from Cuba (also established in South Florida). It needs a tall, humid enclosure with strong UVB. Most are wild-caught and wary, so treat it as a display animal rather than a handling pet.
rows: About 13–17 in total; males are larger
Tall: 24 × 24 × 48 in (L × W × H) minimum for one adult; taller is better. Plenty of branches and foliage
Basking 90–95°F, warm side 80–85°F, cool side 70–80°F, night 65–75°F
High UVB need: a T5 HO UVB tube (e.g. 10–12%) over the basking area
Live insects (crickets, roach nymphs, mealworms, waxworms); occasional fruit and small vertebrates such as pinkie mice. Dust with calcium; multivitamin weekly
Poor: usually distrustful and bites hard when restrained. Best as a display animal
Active by day; arboreal (lives high in trees)
Cuba; introduced and spreading in South Florida
notes: Males are fiercely territorial: never house two males together. Best kept singly.

sources.name: Reptile Direct – Cuban knight anole care sheet
The Tye-Dyed Iguana – Cuban knight anole care sheet

re-basiliscus-plumifrons.title: Green Basilisk (Plumed Basilisk)
re-basiliscus-plumifrons.summary: A large, crested green lizard from humid Central American rainforest streams, famous for sprinting across water on its hind legs. It's nervous and active, needs a very large, tall, humid enclosure with a pool, and is not an impulse pet.
rows: About 24–36 in (70–90 cm) total, mostly tail
About 8–12 years in captivity; some sources say 13+
At least 150 × 75 × 150 cm (about 5 × 2.5 × 5 ft) for one adult, with branches at many heights, dense foliage and a pool big enough to soak and swim. Babies can start in a 40-gal breeder
Basking spot about 95°F, ambient 80–88°F; nights can drop into the high 70s °F
Diurnal: needs bright light and UVB, with true darkness at night
Insectivore: a variety of live insects (crickets, roach nymphs, mealworms, waxworms). Dust with calcium daily, multivitamin weekly
Active by day; jumps, climbs and swims; runs across water to escape
Atlantic side of Central America, eastern Honduras to western Panama (rainforest streams)

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Basiliscus plumifrons care guide
The Tye-Dyed Iguana – Green basilisk care sheet

re-takydromus-sexlineatus.title: Long-Tailed Grass Lizard
re-takydromus-sexlineatus.summary: A small, slender, gentle lizard from Southeast Asian grasslands and open forest whose tail makes up about three-quarters of its length. It's agile, active by day, and one of the easier beginner lizards when given a tall, planted, well-ventilated terrarium.
rows: About 8–10 in (20–25 cm) total; the body is only 2.3–2.7 in, the rest is tail
Tall, well-ventilated, planted terrarium (they climb through plants); floor space for hunting and egg-laying too
Active by day; mostly arboreal, comes to the ground to hunt and lay eggs
Southeast Asia (India and southern China to Indonesia): open forest and shrubby grassland
notes: Fairly social: best kept as 1 male with 3 or more females; two males may fight.
Can drop its tail and regrow it.

sources.name: Exo Terra – Six-striped long-tailed lizard care guide

re-varanus-prasinus.title: Green (Emerald) Tree Monitor
re-varanus-prasinus.summary: A slender, bright green, very active tree-dwelling monitor from New Guinea. It needs a tall, densely furnished enclosure, high humidity and a mostly insect diet, and it's a lizard for experienced keepers, not a handling pet.
rows: About 30–39 in (75–100 cm) total length, mostly tail
One adult: at least about 4 × 2 × 4 ft (120 × 60 × 120 cm), taller is better, with branches, cork tubes, shelves and cover in the upper half. Escape-proof and lockable
About 70–90% with good airflow, dry perches and humid retreats; fresh water dish
Bright light with linear UVB over part of the enclosure (about UVI 2–3 in the upper basking zone); 10–12 hours a day
Insect-eater and carnivore: roaches, crickets, locusts, silkworms and snails, with chicks or small whole prey used sparingly. Keep it lean
Not a handling pet: treat as mildly venomous; bites can cause deep cuts, swelling and infection. Feed with tongs and build trust through routine
New Guinea and nearby islands (humid tropical forest)
notes: Keep singly unless breeding under a controlled plan.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Emerald tree monitor care guide

re-varanus-macraei.title: Blue Tree Monitor
re-varanus-macraei.summary: A striking blue-spotted tree monitor found only on Batanta Island in Indonesia. Like its green cousin, it needs a tall, heavily planted and humid enclosure and a mostly insect diet, and it's a species for specialist keepers.
rows: About 35–43 in (90–110 cm) total length; females are a little smaller
One adult: at least about 4 × 2 × 5 ft (120 × 60 × 150 cm) with climbing routes, cork tubes and shaded retreats. Escape-proof and lockable
About 75–90% with good airflow and dry perches; fresh water dish
Bright light with linear UVB over part of the enclosure (about UVI 2–3 in the upper basking zone); 10–12 hours a day
Insect-eater and carnivore: roaches, crickets, locusts, silkworms and snails, with chicks or small whole prey used sparingly. Keep it lean
Not a handling pet: treat as mildly venomous; bites can cause deep cuts, swelling and infection. Feed with tongs and build trust through routine
notes: Narrow-range island species: buy only documented captive-bred animals.
Keep singly unless breeding under a controlled plan.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Blue tree monitor care guide

re-varanus-salvator.title: Asian Water Monitor
re-varanus-salvator.summary: One of the world's largest lizards, a powerful swimmer from the rivers, swamps and mangroves of South and Southeast Asia. Adults need a room-sized enclosure with a big heated pool, so this is strictly a specialist animal.
rows: Usually about 5–8 ft (1.5–2.5 m) total length; exceptional animals are larger
Room-sized or secure outdoor enclosure with a large, heated, drainable pool; 10 × 6 × 6 ft (300 × 180 × 180 cm) is only a starting point for young adults
Basking area 45–55°C (113–131°F), warm side 29–33°C, cool side 24–28°C, night 22–26°C
About 60–85% with dry resting places and good airflow
Bright light plus UVB (about UVI 3–4 at basking height); 10–12 hours a day
Carnivore: whole prey such as rodents (in moderation), chicks, quail and fish used carefully, occasional eggs, and large insects for juveniles. Avoid overfeeding
Not a handling pet: treat as mildly venomous; bites can cause deep cuts, swelling and infection. Feed with tongs and build trust through routine
Active by day; semi-aquatic and an excellent swimmer
Sri Lanka and eastern India through Southeast Asia to Indonesia and the Philippines
warn: Grows to 5–8 ft or more and needs a room-sized enclosure with a pool.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Asian water monitor care guide
